prompt: The section opens with a general definition of work, w = ∫F·ds. What does this say work is?

choices.text: A force acting along a path, added up over the path
A force divided by the area that it acts on
choices.why: Force per area is pressure, P = F/A. Work combines a force with the distance it acts through, w = ∫F·ds.

choices.text: The energy that flows because of a temperature difference
choices.why: That describes heat, not work. Work is a force acting along a path, w = ∫F·ds.

choices.text: The mass of an object times the speed it moves at
choices.why: Mass times velocity is momentum. Work is a force times a path element, added up along the path.

explanation: Work is the inner product of a force F and a path element ds, integrated along the path. Pushing against friction, moving a charge in an electric field and compressing a gas are all examples.

prompt: Work is the integral of the inner (dot) product F·ds. How much work does a force do if it always acts at right angles to the direction of motion?

choices.text: None, since F·ds is zero
The full force times the distance moved
choices.why: That holds only when the force points along the motion. At right angles, the inner product F·ds is zero.

choices.text: Half the force times the distance moved
choices.why: The inner product doesn't take half of the force. At right angles, F·ds = 0, so no work is done.

choices.text: The force times the distance, but negative
choices.why: A negative F·ds needs a force pointing against the motion. At right angles, F·ds = 0.

explanation: The inner product F·ds keeps only the part of the force that lies along the motion. A force at right angles to the motion has no such part, so it does no work.

prompt: The section writes electrical work as w = ∫eE·ds. What is being moved, and against what?

choices.text: A charge e, against an electric field E
A piston, against the external pressure
choices.why: That is P–V work. In ∫eE·ds, e is a charge and E is the electric field it is moved against.

choices.text: An object, against the force of friction
choices.why: Work against friction is written with the friction force. Electrical work moves a charge e against an electric field E.

choices.text: A magnet, against a magnetic field
choices.why: The section names that as yet another kind of work. In ∫eE·ds, a charge e is moved against an electric field E.

explanation: Electrical work moves a charge e, such as an electron, against an electric field E. The force on the charge is eE, so the work has the same force-along-a-path form, ∫eE·ds.

prompt: Force and path element are both vectors, yet for a gas in a cylinder the section treats the work as a simple product. Why can it do this?

choices.text: The piston moves only one way, along the forces
Force and distance are parallel for every kind of work
choices.why: In general they need not be, which is why work is an inner product. In a cylinder, the piston is held to move along the line of the pressure forces.

choices.text: The piston is massless, so its direction doesn't matter
choices.why: The piston's mass is not the point. The forces act along the piston's only direction of motion, so the inner product becomes a plain product.

choices.text: Pressure is a vector that points the same way as dV
choices.why: Pressure and volume are not vectors here. The work becomes a plain product because the piston moves in one direction, along the forces.

explanation: The piston can only move up or down, and the pressure forces act along that same line. The inner product F·ds then reduces to a plain product of force and distance.

prompt: The section turns the work on a piston of area A, ∫F ds, into ∫P dV. Which two facts does it use?

choices.text: F = PA, and the piston sweeps out a volume dV = A ds
F = P/A, and the piston sweeps out a volume dV = ds/A
choices.why: Pressure is force per area, so F = PA, not P/A. A piston of area A moving through ds sweeps out a volume A ds.

choices.text: F = PV, and the piston sweeps out a volume dV = A ds
choices.why: PV is an energy, not a force. The force on the piston is pressure times area, F = PA.

choices.text: F = PA, and the piston sweeps out a volume dV = A/ds
choices.why: Area divided by a length is a length, not a volume. The volume swept out is the area times the distance, A ds.

explanation: Since P = F/A, the force on the piston is PA, and moving a piston of area A through ds changes the volume by A ds. So F ds = (F/A)(A ds) = P dV.

prompt: Under the section's sign convention, when is the work w positive?

choices.text: When energy is put into the system as work
When the system does work on its surroundings
choices.why: Work the system does takes energy out of it, so it gets a minus sign. Work is positive when energy goes into the system.

choices.text: Whenever the gas in the system expands
choices.why: An expanding gas does work on its surroundings, so its w is negative. Work is positive when energy is put in, as in a compression.

choices.text: Whenever the pressure of the system is positive
choices.why: Gas pressure is always positive, so this would make all P–V work positive. The sign of w depends on whether energy goes into or out of the system.

explanation: Positive heat and positive work are always energy put into the system; energy the system gives off as heat or work gets a minus sign. The section sums this up as “you pay the bill”.

prompt: Under the same sign convention, what sign does q have when a system gives off heat to its surroundings?

choices.text: Negative, since energy leaves the system
Positive, since heat is flowing
choices.why: Heat can flow in either direction, so flow alone doesn't fix the sign. Heat leaving the system is negative.

choices.text: Positive, since the surroundings gain energy
choices.why: The sign is taken from the system's point of view. The system loses energy, so q is negative.

choices.text: It depends on the work the system does
choices.why: The sign of q is set by the direction of the heat flow alone. Heat leaving the system is negative, whatever the work is.

explanation: The convention looks at energy from the system's side: what goes in is positive and what comes out is negative. Heat given off by the system therefore has q < 0.

prompt: The section first writes volume work as ∫P dV, then rewrites it as w = −∫P dV. Why add the minus sign?

choices.text: So that a compression, putting energy in, gives w > 0
Because the pressure of a gas is a negative number
choices.why: Gas pressure is positive. The minus sign makes w positive when the volume shrinks, that is, when work is put into the gas.

choices.text: So that an expanding gas, which does work, gives w > 0
choices.why: That was the sign before the minus was added. With it, an expanding gas has w < 0, because it gives off energy as work.

choices.text: Because work always takes energy out of a system
choices.why: Work can go into or out of a system. The minus sign makes a compression, where work goes in, come out positive.

explanation: With w = −∫P dV, a compression (dV negative) gives positive work, energy put into the gas. An expansion gives negative work, energy the gas gives off.

prompt: A gas at pressure P sits in a cylinder under a piston, with an external pressure P_ext on the other side. When is the gas compressed?

choices.text: When P_ext is greater than P
When P is greater than P_ext
choices.why: Then the gas pushes harder than the outside and the piston moves out, an expansion. Compression needs P_ext > P.

choices.text: When P_ext is equal to P
choices.why: With the pressures equal, the forces balance and the piston stays put. The gas is compressed only when P_ext is greater than P.

choices.text: Whenever P_ext is above 1 bar
choices.why: What matters is how P_ext compares with the gas pressure P, not a fixed value. If P_ext > P, the piston moves in.

explanation: The piston moves toward the side with the lower pressure. If P_ext > P it moves in and compresses the gas; if P_ext < P the gas expands.

prompt: If the external pressure stays constant, what does the work w = −∫P_ext dV become?

choices.text: w = −P_ext ΔV
w = P_ext ΔV
choices.why: This drops the minus sign of the convention. With it, w = −P_ext ΔV, which is positive for a compression.

choices.text: w = −V ΔP_ext
choices.why: P_ext doesn't change here, so this would always give zero. A constant P_ext comes out of the integral, leaving −P_ext ΔV.

choices.text: w = −P_ext/ΔV
choices.why: Pressure divided by volume is not an energy. Taking the constant P_ext out of the integral leaves −P_ext times ΔV.

explanation: A constant P_ext can be taken out of the integral, and the integral of dV from V_1 to V_2 is just ΔV = V_2 − V_1. So w = −P_ext ΔV.

prompt: If the external pressure changes during a compression, how does the section say the work must be found?

choices.text: By integrating P_ext(V) over the volume range
As −P_ext ΔV, using the starting value of P_ext
choices.why: That works only when P_ext stays constant. When it changes, w = −∫P_ext(V) dV over the whole range.

choices.text: As −P_ext ΔV, using the final value of P_ext
choices.why: One value of P_ext can't stand for a pressure that changes. The work is w = −∫P_ext(V) dV over the whole range.

choices.text: As −V ΔP_ext, from the change in P_ext
choices.why: P–V work comes from the volume change, not the pressure change. With a changing P_ext, w = −∫P_ext(V) dV.

explanation: −P_ext ΔV holds only for a constant external pressure. If P_ext changes as V changes, w = −∫P_ext(V) dV must be taken over the whole range from V_1 to V_2.

prompt: A gas is compressed by a constant external pressure that is higher than its own pressure. Why does the section call this process irreversible?

choices.text: Its pressure differs from the pressure on it
No heat can flow into or out of the gas during it
choices.why: That describes an adiabatic process. This one is irreversible because the inside and outside pressures differ, so the gas is out of equilibrium.

choices.text: The volume of the gas can't change at all
choices.why: The volume does change; the gas is compressed. It is irreversible because the gas pressure differs from the pressure on it.

choices.text: The gas always ends up hotter than it started
choices.why: In the section's example the gas starts and ends at the same temperature. It is irreversible because the pressures are unbalanced along the way.

explanation: Because the system pressure is not the pressure exerted on it, the system is not in a state of equilibrium during the change. Such a process is called irreversible.

prompt: For a compression at constant external pressure, what can a P–V diagram show?

choices.text: The work as an area, but not the path itself
The path of the gas, but not the work done
choices.why: It is the other way round. The gas is out of equilibrium during the change, so its path can't be drawn, but the work −P_ext ΔV can be shown as an area.

choices.text: Both the path and the work, as for any change
choices.why: Only states in equilibrium can be drawn on a P–V diagram. The path of this irreversible change can't be shown, though the work can.

choices.text: Neither the path nor the work
choices.why: The work at constant P_ext can still be shown, as the area under the line at P_ext. Only the path itself can't be drawn.

explanation: A P–V diagram shows equilibrium states, and an irreversible change passes through states that are not in equilibrium. The work, −P_ext ΔV, can still be shown as the area under the line at constant P_ext.

prompt: A P–V diagram of a compression at constant external pressure also shows the isotherm, a curve of constant temperature, through the starting state 1. The final state 2 lies on the same isotherm. What does this tell you?

choices.text: The gas ends at the same temperature it started at
The gas followed the isotherm during the compression
choices.why: The irreversible path can't be drawn at all. The isotherm only shows that states 1 and 2 have the same temperature.

choices.text: The gas pressure stayed constant during the compression
choices.why: The gas pressure rises from state 1 to state 2; only P_ext is constant. Sharing an isotherm means the two states have the same temperature.

choices.text: No work was done on the gas in the compression
choices.why: Work was done; it is the area under the line at P_ext. Being on one isotherm only means the temperatures at 1 and 2 are equal.

explanation: An isotherm connects states with the same temperature. With states 1 and 2 on it, the irreversible compression starts and ends at the same temperature, even though its path in between can't be drawn.

prompt: Moving an object against friction is one kind of work. For a constant force along the path, w = ∫F·ds becomes force × distance. How much work, in J, does it take to push a box 3.0 m across a floor against a friction force of 40 N?
explanation: w = F × distance = 40 N × 3.0 m = 120 J. One joule is one newton-metre.

prompt: A gas pushes a piston of area 0.0200 m^2 outward by 0.100 m against a constant external pressure of 1.00 × 10^5 Pa, so its volume grows by ΔV = area × distance. Using w = −P_ext ΔV, what is w, in J?
explanation: ΔV = 0.0200 m^2 × 0.100 m = 0.00200 m^3, so w = −(1.00 × 10^5 Pa)(0.00200 m^3) = −200 J. It is negative because the gas gives off energy as work.

prompt: A gas is compressed from 4.0 L to 1.0 L by a constant external pressure of 3.0 bar. Using w = −P_ext ΔV and 1 L·bar = 100 J, what is w, in J?
explanation: ΔV = 1.0 L − 4.0 L = −3.0 L, so w = −(3.0 bar)(−3.0 L) = 9.0 L·bar = 900 J. It is positive because work is put into the gas.

prompt: A gas is compressed in two steps: first from 5.0 L to 3.0 L at a constant P_ext of 2.0 bar, then from 3.0 L to 2.0 L at a constant P_ext of 4.0 bar. Adding w = −P_ext ΔV for the two steps, and using 1 L·bar = 100 J, what is the total work done on the gas, in J?
explanation: Step 1 gives −(2.0 bar)(−2.0 L) = 4.0 L·bar, and step 2 gives −(4.0 bar)(−1.0 L) = 4.0 L·bar. The total is 8.0 L·bar = 800 J, which shows why a changing P_ext has to be followed over the whole volume range.

prompt: A gas expands against a constant external pressure of 1.00 bar and does 250 J of work on its surroundings, so w = −250 J. Using w = −P_ext ΔV and 1 L·bar = 100 J, by how many liters did its volume increase? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: w = −250 J = −2.50 L·bar, so ΔV = −w/P_ext = 2.50 L·bar ÷ 1.00 bar = 2.50 L. The volume grows, as it must when a gas does work on its surroundings.
